background.definition: Giardiasis is a parasitic infection caused by Giardia sp., a flagellated enteric protozoan, which typically presents as an acute and/or chronic diarrheal illness.

list.listitem: Approximately 15,000 to 24,000 cases are reported in the United States annually, with numbers declining in recent years.
Disease estimates are much higher because of suspected underreporting.
Giardia and Cryptosporidium are the two most common intestinal parasites in the United States, and are very common worldwide.
Giardiasis varies by patient population; it is most commonly seen in children.
Giardia lamblia, also called Giardia intestinalis and Giardia duodenalis.
The Giardia cyst is the hardy, highly infectious form of the protozoan that can survive for long periods in moist conditions, including chlorinated water.
The cyst may be ingested from contaminated food or water or by person-to-person spread, particularly among young children with poor fecal-oral hygiene.

After ingestion of the cyst, the trophozoite form is released in the upper small bowel, where it replicates and adheres to the mucosal wall. Since it does not invade the mucosa, the pathogenesis of diarrhea and malabsorption is not entirely understood.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Age: children younger than 5 years, in daycare
Contact with contaminated recreational, surface, and well water, as with camping or traveling to endemic areas
Immunocompromised state, including absence of secretory IgA, which is important for clearing the intestinal infection
Hypochlorhydria, as with previous gastric surgery or reduced gastric acidity
Contact with infected animals, primarily pets

list.listitem: Measures to prevent infection include: good hygiene, proper food handling, boiling water for at least 10 minutes at 70°C or greater, treating water with iodine for 8 hours or more, and using water microfilters with 1-mcg pore size. C
Decontamination of water with iodine for at least 8 hours is more effective than chlorination. C
Test for Giardia and other parasites when diarrhea persists beyond 7 days. C
Microscopic identification of three separate stool samples for cysts or trophozoites is 90% sensitive for Giardia. C
PCR is more sensitive than light microscopy, if available. C
Stool antigen assays are the preferred test in many laboratories, with sensitivity ranging from 85% to 98% and specificity from 90% to 100%. C
Since lactose intolerance develops in 20% to 40% of cases of giardiasis, perform additional stool examinations to confirm persistent infection or reinfection. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, and Escherichia coli 0157:H7
Differential.Differential_Features: These 4 organisms typically produce bloody diarrhea, whereas Giardia does not

Differential.Differential_Name: Yersinia, Vibrio, Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, and E. coli 0157:H7
Differential.Differential_Features: Stool samples from patients with these infections usually have fecal leukocytes; giardia does not

Giardia can be difficult to distinguish from Cryptosporidium as the epidemiology of the 2 is quite similar. Giardia tends to produce a greasier diarrhea whereas Cryptosporidium typically causes a more watery diarrhea

Organisms other than Giardia that can cause chronic GI infection include Cryptosporidium, Campylobacter, Clostridium difficile, Cyclospora, Aeromonas, Plesiomonas, and amebae; Whipple’s disease also causes GI infection

list.listitem: Giardiasis occurs most often in the summer through early fall.

Symptoms typically develop 7 to 14 days after inoculation. Clinical manifestations are quite variable, ranging from asymptomatic disease in up to 60% of those infected to severe infection requiring hospitalization.

Symptoms include acute onset of loose, greasy diarrhea, malaise, flatulence, steatorrhea, abdominal cramps, bloating, nausea, anorexia, and weight loss. Occasionally, urticaria, constipation, reactive arthritis, biliary tract disease, and gastritis have been reported.
Symptoms typically last more than a week. Giardiasis can become a chronic infection in up to half of all symptomatic patients.

Chronic infection does not require a preceding symptomatic acute phase and has a similar symptom profile to acute infection, but with greasier stools, profound malaise, lassitude, weight loss, and depression.
Malabsorption can be particularly problematic, with resultant vitamin deficiencies and secondary lactase deficiency, leading to worsening diarrhea with dairy consumption.
Microscopic identification of the cysts or trophozoites in fresh stool is the gold standard for diagnosis.
Examine multiple samples, as Giardia is identified in only 50% of single stool samples; the yield increases to 90% with the examination of 3 stool specimens.
Stool antigen assays may be the preferred test in many laboratories, with sensitivity ranging from 85% to 98%; and specificity from 90% to 100%.

A systematic review of 34 stsudies of immunoassays found that ImmunoCardSTAT (84% sensitivity, 99% specificity, LR+ 84, LR- 0.16) and RIDASCREEN Giardia (93% sensitive, 99% specific, LR+ 93, LR- 0.07) were most accurate.

Immunoassays and PCR are increasingly used but are not as helpful in the initial evaluation of acute diarrhea. A recombinase polymerase amplification-based assay was 73% sensitive and 95% specific compared with PCR.
PCR is probably superior to light microscopy but is not as widely available as microscopy or antigen assay.
Costs for immunoassay and microscopic examination are comparable but may be higher with microscopy using special staining and multiple specimens.
Other laboratory tests including peripheral white cell count or eosinophilia are not helpful.
IgM and IgG antibodies persist after previous infection so are not helpful in the evaluation of acute diarrheal illness.
Radiography may show nonspecific mucosal edema and is typically not helpful.
Since lactose intolerance develops in 20% to 40% of cases of giardiasis, perform additional stool examination to confirm persisting infection or reinfection.
In the initial evaluation of acute or chronic diarrhea, Giardia should be suspected in patients who have the risk factors noted above.
Testing for Giardia and other parasites is recommended when diarrhea persists beyond 7 days.

Because of similar risk factors and clinical presentation Giardia may easily be confused with Cryptosporidium. Examination of the stool and/or PCR or immunoassay can distinguish the infecting organisms.
Metronidazole and tinidazole are the least expensive treatments with high efficacy. B

Treatment options for persistent giardial infection include another course of the same drug for either a longer time period or with a higher dose, switching to a different drug class, or combination therapy including metronidazole and quinacrine. B
Avoid dairy products for 1 month following treatment due to the high rate of secondary lactose intolerance. C
It is important to treat asymptomatic infection in patients at risk of transmitting disease, such as food handlers.
Metronidazole is the traditional drug of choice for Giardiasis but is not FDA approved for this indication.
One dose of tinidazole is highly effective (clinical cure rate over 90%), with fewer adverse effects reported.

Side effects are similar for both agents, including metallic taste, indigestion, nausea and vomiting, disulfiram-like effect, muscle cramps, blood dyscrasia, and neurologic symptoms ranging from headache and dizziness to peripheral neuropathy and seizure.
Metronidazole is the least expensive, but the costs of both tinidazole and metronidazole are generally under $25 per treatment.
Other treatment options include nitazoxanide, quinacrine, furazolidone, albendazole, paromomycin, and bacitracin-zinc (see ).

A recent Cochrane review concluded that albendazole (400 mg daily for 5-10 days) is of similar efficacy as metronidazole (25-500 mg three times daily for 5-10 days), but with fewer adverse effects and a more simplified regimen.
Because of the possibility of lactose intolerance, patients should avoid dairy products for 1 month after treatment.
Probiotics may be effective although the evidence base is poor.

Options for treating persistent giardiasis include another course of the same drug for either a longer time period or with a higher dose, switching to a different drug class, or combination therapy including metronidazole and quinacrine.
Lactose intolerance develops in 20% to 40% of cases of giardiasis, requiring additional stool examination to rule out persisting infection or reinfection.
Giardiasis may be acute and self-limiting or may develop into a chronic diarrheal illness leading to complications secondary to malabsorption and dehydration. C
Lactose intolerance develops in 20% to 40% of cases. B
Infection may be acute and self-limited or may become chronic, possibly leading to persistent diarrhea, profound malaise, lassitude, weight loss, and depression.
Prognosis with appropriate treatment is good.
Specific follow-up is unnecessary unless symptoms persist or if proof of cure is needed in special circumstances (eg, for a food handler).
Good hygiene, including proper food handling and hand washing, is important to prevent person-to-person spread.
Instruct patients to boil potentially infected water for at least 10 minutes (70°C or greater).
Water treated with iodine for at least 8 hours is safe.
Some commercially available water filters may be effective.
Instruct patients to seek medical advice for diarrhea lasting longer than 7 days.
No vaccine is available.
Delay treatment in women with mild symptoms until after delivery or at least until after the first trimester.
The recommended drug is paromomycin (pregnancy category C) for use in symptomatic pregnant women.

Do not use metronidazole and tinidazole in the first trimester of pregnancy, and use them with caution in the second and third trimester, only when symptoms are severe, causing malabsorption and dehydration.
The recommended drugs for treatment in children are metronidazole or tinidazole. See for dosing.
